name: Neyyadiappar Temple, Thillaisthanam
deity: Shiva as Neyyadiappar, a self-manifested lingam, with the goddess Balambigai (Ilamangai Ammai)
period: Seventh and last shrine of the Saptha Sthanam of Thiruvaiyaru; sung in the Tevaram (7th century), with inscriptions from the 9th century
dynasty: Pallava and Chola, with gifts from Pandya and other rulers
summary: At Thillaisthanam on the Kaveri, Shiva is Neyyadiappar, the lord bathed in ghee, and his temple is the last of the seven shrines the Saptha Sthanam procession visits before it turns back to Thiruvaiyaru.

sections.history: Thillaisthanam lies on the northern bank of the Kaveri, about two kilometres west of Thiruvaiyaru on the road towards Thirukattupalli. Its old name was Thiruneithanam, the sacred place of ghee, and the present name is read as a softening of Thiru-nei-sthanam. Appar and Sambandar sang of its lord, making it a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Kaveri's north bank. Its inscriptions reach far back: the earliest is dated to 862 CE, and a record of the Pallava king Nandivarman III gives sixty kalanju of gold for lamps. The stone temple is attributed to the age of the Chola king Aditya I, and Chola, Pandya, Chera and Irukkuvel rulers all added gifts.
sections.architecture: An east-facing rajagopuram opens onto a broad first enclosure, and the sanctum holds a swayambhu lingam, revered as having arisen of itself rather than being carved and installed. The goddess Balambigai, known in Tamil as Ilamangai Ammai, the young lady, has her own shrine. The Kaveri, flowing close by, serves as the temple's sacred water, and the inscribed courses on the walls quietly record more than eleven centuries of devotion.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of a cow that went each day to one spot and let her milk flow there, and the milk turned to ghee. A king, hearing of the wonder, had the ground dug up and found a lingam that had appeared of itself. Because the lord was then bathed in ghee, he came to be called Neyyadiappar, from nei, the Tamil word for ghee. The practice continues to this day: the lingam is anointed with ghee and then with warm water.
sections.festivals: Thillaisthanam is the seventh and last temple of the Saptha Sthanam festival in Chithirai (April–May); here the procession completes its round of the villages before turning back towards Thiruvaiyaru, and the temple stays open late into the night as the palanquins arrive. Tradition holds that the village sent ghee for Nandi's wedding. Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March) and Thiruvathirai in Margazhi (December–January) are also kept with devotion. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Come early to see the ghee abhishekam, the rite that gives the temple its name, and then walk down to the Kaveri, which flows past the village. Thillaisthanam is the nearest of the Saptha Sthanam temples to Thiruvaiyaru, so it pairs easily with a visit to Aiyarappar. On the festival night the riverside village fills with pilgrims waiting to greet the palanquins.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thillaisthanam is about 2 km west of Thiruvaiyaru on the road to Thirukattupalli, and around 15 km from Thanjavur; local buses, autos and taxis come from Thiruvaiyaru. Thanjavur is the nearest major railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport, about 60 km away, is the nearest airport.
